title: Zen and the arts
hookLine: tea, gardens, ink painting and poetry shaped by practice

cards: A bowl of green tea, turned once before it's handed over. A garden with no water in it, only raked gravel and a few stones. A circle drawn in black ink with one stroke.
A short poem about an old pond and a frog jumping in. None of these look like religion: no altar, no sermon, no scripture read aloud.
Yet in Japan, people have tied each of them to Zen practice, to monks and to the people who sat with them. Today: how sitting still spilled out into the hands.

teach.b: The idea underneath is simple. If awakening isn't somewhere else, it can show up in anything done fully. Take tea.
In the tea way, every move is set: how you fold the cloth, how you whisk, how you turn the bowl before you offer it. The rules aren't fussy for their own sake.
They clear the room, so attention has nothing left to do but be here. A saying in the tea world puts it plainly: tea and Zen, one taste. Then the dry garden.

Raked gravel can be read as water, stones as islands or mountains, and some of these gardens are made to be sat beside rather than walked through. The raking itself is practice, done again tomorrow and the day after.
Zen teachers have painted the enso, a circle made in a single movement of the brush. You can't go back and fix it. The circle shows the state of the hand that made it, wobble and all.
And the short poem catches one moment so plainly it hardly seems to have an author. Two threads run through all of these.
Simplicity: take away until what's left is enough. Presence: the thing is done now, once, with the whole person. Japanese has a word for the beauty of what's plain, worn and imperfect: wabi.
A cracked tea bowl, carefully mended, can be prized above a flawless one. Not every artist was a monk, and not every cup of tea is Zen.
But the arts gave practice somewhere to live outside the meditation hall.

how: Zen temples in Japan keep tea gatherings, dry gardens and brush calligraphy as part of temple life, and lay students learn the tea way, ink painting and flower arranging as disciplines of attention.

games.q: you've just drawn an ink circle in one stroke, and it wobbles. what do you do?
o: throw it away and start again until it's perfect.
games.why: the enso is left as it is. it shows the state of the hand that made it, wobble and all.

practice: Pour a glass of water, fold a napkin, or draw one circle on a scrap of paper, once, slowly, with your whole attention, and don't fix it afterward.
Look at what you made, let your hands rest open in your lap, and if the mind wants to redo it, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Wabi. The Japanese word for the beauty of what's plain, worn and imperfect, found in tea, gardens, ink and poems shaped by Zen practice.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyana, meditation. By way of the Chinese Chan, it gives the Japanese word Zen.

carryVoice: Your line: practice in the arts. Anything done fully can hold it. See you tomorrow.
